title: Normal anatomy on radiographs
blurb: Radiolucent versus radiopaque, the normal structures around a tooth, and the landmarks you'll see on every panoramic radiograph.
question: A patient looking at her panoramic radiograph on the screen points to two large dark areas above her upper back teeth and a white line running down the middle of her nose, and asks if something is wrong. What are these, and why do they look the way they do?

teach.body: A radiograph is a map of how much X-ray energy got through. Where little material is in the way (air, soft tissue, the pulp), X-rays reach the receptor and the image is dark: this is radiolucent. Where dense material absorbs them (enamel, bone, metal fillings), less reaches the receptor and the image is white or light grey: this is radiopaque. Every structure you learn to recognise is simply a pattern of radiolucent and radiopaque shapes.

bands.label: Gums, cheeks, tongue, pulp, PDL space

teach.caption: On a periapical: enamel is the whitest part of the tooth, the pulp chamber and canals are radiolucent, a thin dark line around the root is the periodontal ligament (PDL) space, and a thin white line outside it lining the socket is the lamina dura.

Look for the vertical white nasal septum in the midline, the horizontal white line of the hard palate, the dark maxillary sinuses above the upper back teeth, the thick white inferior border of the mandible, and the hyoid shadows low down on each side.

teach.h: A map of the panoramic image
teach.caption: Dark cells are radiolucent landmarks; light cells are radiopaque. A DPT is viewed as if facing the patient, so the patient's right is on your left.

teach.body: The mandibular canal carries the inferior alveolar nerve and blood vessels. Before a lower wisdom tooth is removed or an implant placed, the dentist checks how close the roots or implant site are to it, because damage can leave the lip numb. The mental foramen, a small dark spot near the lower premolar apices, and the maxillary sinus close to upper molar roots can both be mistaken for disease by the untrained eye. Knowing normal anatomy is what lets the team spot when something isn't normal.

teach.text: Radioluc-ENT = X-rays went through = DARK. Radio-OPAQUE = opaque to X-rays = WHITE. Air-filled spaces like the sinuses are radiolucent; bone borders like the inferior border of the mandible are radiopaque.

items: Radiolucent = dark (air, soft tissue, pulp); radiopaque = white (enamel, bone, metal).
Around a tooth: radiolucent PDL space and pulp; radiopaque lamina dura and enamel.
DPT: dark maxillary sinuses, white nasal septum and hard palate, white inferior border of the mandible.
Dark mandibular canal below the molar roots (inferior alveolar nerve); coronoid ahead of the condyle; hyoid shadows below the jaw.

summary: You can now explain radiolucent and radiopaque, recognise the normal structures around a tooth, and find the maxillary sinuses, nasal septum, hard palate, inferior border, mandibular canal, coronoid process and hyoid shadows on a panoramic radiograph.

A.q: On a panoramic radiograph, what are the large dark areas above the upper posterior teeth on both sides?
A.why: The maxillary sinuses are air-filled spaces above the upper back teeth, so they appear radiolucent (dark).

whyNot.0: The orbits lie much higher, at the top edge of the image.
whyNot.1: The nasal septum is a single vertical white line in the midline.
whyNot.2: The mandibular canals are in the lower jaw, below the molar roots.

options: Appears dark because X-rays pass through
Appears white because X-rays are absorbed
Appears grey because of soft tissue
A.why: Radiopaque structures absorb X-rays, so less reaches the receptor and they appear white.

whyNot.0: Dark areas where X-rays pass through are radiolucent.
whyNot.1: Blurring is a movement fault, not a description of density.
whyNot.3: Soft tissue appears dark grey and is relatively radiolucent.

A.q: Which structure runs as a radiolucent channel below the lower molar roots, carrying the inferior alveolar nerve?
A.why: The mandibular canal carries the inferior alveolar nerve and vessels and shows as a dark channel with thin white borders.

whyNot.1: The maxillary sinus is in the upper jaw.
whyNot.2: The hyoid is a radiopaque bone in the neck, below the mandible.
whyNot.3: The coronoid process is a bony projection of the ramus, not a channel.

B.q: What is the vertical radiopaque line in the centre of the nasal cavity on a DPT?
B.why: The nasal septum divides the nasal cavity and appears as a vertical white line in the midline.

whyNot.0: The hard palate is a horizontal white line above the upper tooth roots.
whyNot.1: The inferior border is the lower outline of the mandible.
whyNot.3: The lamina dura is the thin white lining of each tooth socket.

B.q: Which of these appears MOST radiopaque on a dental radiograph?
B.why: Metal such as amalgam absorbs almost all the X-rays and appears bright white, whiter even than enamel.

whyNot.0: The pulp is soft tissue and appears radiolucent.
whyNot.1: The sinus is air-filled and appears dark.
whyNot.2: The periodontal ligament space is a thin radiolucent line around the root.

B.q: What is the pointed upward projection at the front of the mandibular ramus, ahead of the condyle?
B.why: The coronoid process projects upwards from the front of the ramus, anterior to the condyle.

whyNot.1: The mental foramen is a small radiolucent opening near the lower premolar apices.
whyNot.2: The hyoid bone lies below the mandible in the neck.
whyNot.3: The angle is the lower back corner of the mandible, not an upward projection.

C.q: On a DPT, what are the rounded radiopaque shadows seen low down on each side, beneath the mandible?
C.why: The hyoid bone sits in the neck below the mandible and commonly shows as radiopaque shadows on each side.

whyNot.0: Salivary stones aren't a normal finding and would not appear symmetrically on both sides as standard.
whyNot.1: The condyles sit at the top of the rami, near the ears.
whyNot.3: Earrings should be removed and would appear higher, near the ear lobes.

C.q: What is the curved radiopaque border forming the lower outline of the mandible called?
C.why: The inferior border of the mandible is thick cortical bone, seen as a curved white outline along the bottom of the jaw.

whyNot.0: The external oblique ridge runs across the ramus and body higher up.
whyNot.1: The mylohyoid line is on the inner surface of the mandible, not its lower edge.
whyNot.2: The lamina dura lines individual tooth sockets.

C.q: Around a healthy root on a periapical, what is the thin radiolucent line between the root and the socket wall?
C.why: The periodontal ligament is soft tissue, so the space it fills appears as a thin dark line around the root.

whyNot.1: The lamina dura is the thin radiopaque (white) line lining the socket.
whyNot.2: The root canal runs inside the root, not around it.
whyNot.3: Enamel covers the crown and appears very radiopaque.

reteach.title: Shadows on a wall
reteach.question: If you shine a torch through objects onto a wall, why do some cast dark shadows and others let the light through?

blocks.body: With a torch, solid objects make dark shadows. A radiograph works the other way round: the receptor turns dark wherever X-rays hit it, so anything that blocks X-rays leaves a WHITE 'shadow'. Bone and teeth block them, so they look white. Air-filled spaces like the sinuses block almost nothing, so they look black. Think of the sinuses as empty rooms (dark) and the inferior border of the mandible as a thick wall (white).

blocks.text: Blocked X-rays = white. Passed-through X-rays = dark. Air is the darkest thing on any radiograph; metal is the whitest.

explain.body: Radiolucent areas let X-rays through and look dark: air, soft tissue, the pulp. Radiopaque areas absorb X-rays and look white: enamel, bone, metal restorations.

test.q: Why does a maxillary sinus appear dark on a radiograph?
options: It is full of dense bone
It is out of the beam
test.why: Air absorbs very few X-rays, so the receptor behind it is strongly exposed and appears dark (radiolucent).

whyNot.2: Areas outside the beam would be unexposed, not anatomical dark shapes.

explain.body: Enamel is the whitest natural tissue, dentine slightly less so, and the pulp is dark. A thin dark PDL space surrounds the root, with the thin white lamina dura lining the socket outside it.

options: A dark line inside the root
The white lining of the socket
The enamel cap of the crown
test.why: The lamina dura is the thin layer of dense bone lining the socket, seen as a radiopaque line around the root.

whyNot.0: The dark line inside the root is the root canal.
whyNot.2: The enamel cap is part of the tooth, not the socket.
whyNot.3: Tongue shadows are soft-tissue outlines, not the lamina dura.

explain.body: Maxillary sinuses: large dark areas above the upper back teeth. Nasal septum: vertical white line in the midline. Hard palate: horizontal white line just above the upper roots.

explain.caption: Find the dark sinuses and white nasal septum near the top.

test.q: Which landmark appears as a horizontal radiopaque line just above the roots of the upper teeth on a DPT?
test.why: The hard palate is a plate of bone that shows as a horizontal white line above the upper tooth roots.

whyNot.1: The mandibular canal is dark and lies in the lower jaw.
whyNot.2: The inferior border is the bottom edge of the mandible.
whyNot.3: The hyoid is below the mandible in the neck.

explain.body: Inferior border: thick white curve along the bottom of the mandible. Mandibular canal: dark channel below the molar roots. Coronoid process: pointed projection ahead of the condyle. Hyoid: white shadows below the jaw.

test.q: Why does the dentist check the mandibular canal before removing a lower wisdom tooth?
options: It marks the maxillary sinus floor
It holds the inferior alveolar nerve
It shows where the tongue rests
test.why: The canal carries the inferior alveolar nerve; roots close to it raise the risk of nerve injury and lip numbness.

whyNot.0: The parotid duct opens in the cheek and isn't in the mandible.
whyNot.1: The maxillary sinus is in the upper jaw.
whyNot.3: The tongue's position has nothing to do with the canal.
